title: Shyam Metalics Surges After Q1 Profit Jumps 21% as Goldman and UBS Name It a Top Midcap Pick
excerpt: The Kolkata-based steelmaker posted its strongest quarterly performance in three years, prompting Goldman Sachs to initiate coverage with a Buy rating and UBS to flag it as their top midcap idea.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Shyam Metalics' Q1 FY27 net profit rose 21% to ₹351 crore, with revenue at ₹5,502 crore.
  • Goldman Sachs initiated coverage with a Buy rating and a price target of ₹1,065.
  • UBS named Shyam Metalics its top midcap pick, citing low debt and diversified products.
  • The company's debt-to-equity ratio stands at approximately 0.07, among the lowest in the sector.
  • Shyam Metalics' stock gained about 45% over the past year, outperforming major indices.

Q1 FY27 results from Shyam Metalics
  • Shyam Metalics reported Q1 FY27 net profit of ₹351 crore, up 21% year-on-year, with revenue reaching ₹5,502 crore
  • Goldman Sachs initiated coverage with a Buy rating and price target of ₹1,065, citing expansion into value-added steel products
  • UBS named the stock its top midcap pick in Indian metals, highlighting the company's near-zero debt and diversified product mix
  • The company operates with a debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.07, among the lowest in the Indian steel sector

Shyam Metalics and Energy, the Kolkata-headquartered integrated steel producer, has emerged as Wall Street's newest favourite in the Indian metals space after reporting a sharp jump in quarterly profits and drawing bullish initiations from two of the world's largest investment banks.

Q1 FY27 Results

The company posted a consolidated net profit of ₹351 crore for Q1 FY27, a 21% increase from the same quarter last year. Revenue came in at ₹5,502 crore. For the full financial year FY26, Shyam Metalics had delivered revenue of ₹4,419 crore — a 22.4% jump year-on-year — with EBITDA of ₹580 crore (up 18.8%) and a profit surge of 32% on a sequential quarter-over-quarter basis in Q4.

The results reflect the company's strategy of shifting its product mix toward higher-margin value-added steel products, including TMT bars, structural steel, and ferro alloys, while maintaining its position in pellets and sponge iron.

Goldman Sachs and UBS Weigh In

Goldman Sachs initiated coverage on Shyam Metalics with a Buy rating and a 12-month price target of ₹1,065 — implying roughly 28% upside from current levels. The bank cited the company's integrated operations from mines to finished products, its expansion into higher-value segments, and what it called an "exceptionally clean balance sheet."

UBS went further, designating Shyam Metalics as its top midcap pick within the Indian metals and mining sector. The Swiss bank highlighted the company's debt-to-equity ratio of approximately 0.07 — among the lowest in the Indian steel industry — and noted its rare combination of growth and capital discipline.

"Shyam Metalics offers a rare combination in Indian metals: genuine volume growth, margin expansion from value-added products, and near-zero leverage."

— Goldman Sachs initiating coverage note

What Makes It Stand Out

In an Indian steel industry plagued by cyclicality and heavy debt, Shyam Metalics operates as something of an outlier. The company's integrated model — from captive iron ore and coal mines through to finished long steel products — gives it structural cost advantages that insulate margins during commodity downturns. Its virtually debt-free balance sheet means it can fund expansion internally, avoiding the dilution or leverage that has tripped up competitors like JSW Steel and Tata Steel during previous cycles.

The stock has gained roughly 45% over the past year, outperforming both the Nifty Metal Index and the broader Nifty 50.

What to Watch

Key risks include iron ore price volatility, potential government interventions on steel exports, and execution on capacity expansion plans. For NRI investors who follow Indian midcaps, the dual Goldman-UBS endorsement marks a notable inflection point — institutional foreign interest in Indian midcap steel names has historically been limited.
